value.overview: The Black-crowned Night Heron is a stocky, medium-sized heron found across much of the world. It is named for its mainly nocturnal feeding habits and distinctive black crown and back in adults. This adaptable species uses freshwater and coastal wetlands, often roosting quietly in trees during the day. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon but regular wetland bird, occurring in suitable habitats rather than being one of the country’s most frequently seen herons.
value.classification: The Black-crowned Night Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and the genus Nycticorax. Its scientific name is Nycticorax nycticorax.
value.identification: Adults have a black crown and back, pale gray wings, a whitish face and underparts, red eyes, a thick dark bill, and yellowish legs. Two or three long white plumes extend from the back of the head during the breeding season. Juveniles are brown overall with prominent pale streaks and spots, making them look unlike adults. The species has a compact body, broad rounded wings, and a short tail. Its harsh, barking call is often heard at dusk or night.
value.rangeHabitat: The Black-crowned Night Heron has a broad distribution in North and South America, Europe, Africa, and Asia. It occupies marshes, swamps, ponds, lakes, rivers, lagoons, mangroves, tidal flats, canals, rice fields, and other shallow-water habitats, with trees or dense vegetation nearby for roosting and nesting. In Costa Rica, it is recorded in lowland wetlands and along rivers, lakes, lagoons, mangroves, and other suitable aquatic areas. It is considered uncommon but regular there, including sites such as Caño Negro.
value.migrationStatus: Costa Rica supports both resident or locally occurring birds and migrants from farther north. Northern populations commonly move south after breeding, and some reach Central America during the nonbreeding season. The species is therefore present in Costa Rica year-round in suitable areas, but numbers and visibility may increase during migration and winter.
value.breeding: Black-crowned Night Herons usually breed in colonies, sometimes alongside other herons, egrets, ibises, or gulls. Nests are loose platforms of sticks, reeds, and twigs placed in trees, shrubs, marsh vegetation, or occasionally on the ground. A clutch commonly contains three to five pale bluish or greenish eggs, which hatch asynchronously after about three to four weeks. Both adults care for the young. In Costa Rica, breeding activity has been reported mainly during the rainy-season period, including July and August.
value.dietFeeding: The diet is varied but often includes fish, frogs, aquatic insects, crustaceans, mollusks, small mammals, snakes, and other small aquatic or wetland animals. The heron usually hunts by standing still or walking slowly at the edge of shallow water, then thrusting its bill at prey. It feeds most actively from dusk through the night, although breeding birds may also forage during daylight.
value.behavior: During the day, Black-crowned Night Herons commonly remain motionless in trees, shrubs, reeds, or other sheltered vegetation, often in groups. They become more active at dusk, flying to nearby feeding sites with steady wingbeats and giving loud, harsh calls. They are generally patient ambush hunters and may defend a small feeding area. The species commonly nests and roosts communally, while pairs defend the immediate area around their nest.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered broadly stable, although trends vary among regions. Some local populations have declined, while others have stabilized or increased after earlier pesticide-related losses.
